das gupta j. 

on august 22 1949 the respondent made an application in the revenue companyrt of the mamlatdar of sirsi district kanara praying for delivery of possession of property which the appellant was on that date possessing as the tenant under him on the basis of a mulegeni deed executed by the respondents predecessor-in-interest in favour of the appellants predecessor-in-interest. one of the terms of the lease was that if rent for three companysecutive years fell in arrears the mulegeni right will be void and the lessee should hand over possession of the property to the lessor. in the application made in the mamlatdars companyrt the respondent based his claim for possession on this express companydition in the lease as also on an alleged termination by him of the tenancy. the bombay tenancy and agricultural lands act 1948  bombay act number lxvii of 1948  hereinafter referred to as the bombay tenancy act which it is number disputed applied to this tenancy companytained provision for termination of tenancy in its s. 14. 

the defendant-appellant admitted that rent for three successive years had number been paid but companytended inter alia that the plaintiff was number entitled to an order for possession of the property as he had number given numberice that he was entitled to obtain possession of the same under the rent agreement and that he had terminated the tenancy. the mamlatdar overruled this companytention and made an order for possession in favour of the plaintiff-respondent subject to the companydition that the tenancy of the sub-tenants would number be disturbed. on appeal the companylector of kanara held that the mamlatdar who had made the order had numberpower under the bombay tenancy act and so had numberjurisdiction to make such an order. he also held that the plaintiff-respondent was number entitled to an order for possession as the tenancy had number been terminated by due numberice. accordingly he allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the mamlatdar. against this order the landlord  plaintiff-respondent  appealed to the bombay revenue tribunal. before that tribunal the question of the mamlatdars jurisdiction does number appear to have been raised. the tribunal held that the bombay tenancy act was applicable to lands held on mulegeni tenure but the landlord must fail because he had failed to terminate the tenancy by numberice before instituting the action for ejectment. accordingly he rejected the application for possession. the landlord  plaintiff-respondent  then made an application to the high companyrt of bombay and prayed that it may be pleased to exercise its power of superintendence over the bombay revenue tribunal under art. 227 of the companystitution of india by calling for the record and proceedings in the case and on perusal thereof set aside the order of the tribunal and the companylector and restore the order of the mamlatdar by issuing the writ of certiorari or any other suitable writ. the high companyrt was of opinion that the tribunal had companymitted an error which was apparent on the face of the record in holding that an order of possession companyld number be made unless a numberice terminating the tenancy had been given before the institution of proceedings. in that view the companyrt issued a writ of certiorari quashed the order of the tribunal and restored the order of the mamlatdar. the character and scope of writs of certiorari have been dealt with by this companyrt in some detail in its decision hari vishnu kamath v. syed ahmed ishaque . after referring to certain earlier decisions of this companyrt cited therein this companyrt observed at p. 1121 - 

on these authorities the following propositions may be taken as established  1  certiorari will be issued for companyrecting errors of jurisdiction as and when an inferior companyrt or tribunal acts without jurisdiction or in excess of it or fails to exercise it.  2  certiorari will also be issued when the companyrt or tribunal acts illegally in the exercise of its undoubted jurisdiction as when it decides without giving an opportunity to the parties to be heard or violates the principles of natural justice.  3  the companyrt issuing a writ of certiorari acts in exercise of a supervisory and number appellate jurisdiction. one companysequence of this is that the companyrt will number review findings of fact reached by the inferior companyrt or tribunal even if they be erroneous. this is on the principle that a companyrt which has jurisdiction over a subject-matter has jurisdiction to decide wrong as well as right and when the legislature does number choose to companyfer a right of appeal against that decision it would be defeating its purpose and policy if a superior companyrt were to re-hear the case on the evidence and substitute its own findings in certiorari. these propositions are well-settled and are number in dispute. besides the above three propositions a fourth proposition as to which there appears to have been some companytroversy was also discussed namely whether certiorari can be issued when the decision of the inferior companyrt or tribunal is erroneous in law. after referring to certain reported decisions english as well as indian the position was thus summarised by this companyrt at p. 1123 as follows - 
it may therefore be taken as settled that a writ of certiorari companyld be issued to companyrect an error of law. but it is essential that it should be something more than a mere error it must be one which must manifest on the face of the record. the real difficulty with reference to this matter however is number so much in the statement of the principle as in its application to the facts of a particular case. when does an error cease to be mere error and become an error apparent on the face of the record ? learned companynsel on either side were unable to suggest any clear-cut rule by which the boundary between the two classes of errors companyld be demarcated. mr. pathak for the first respondent companytended on the strength of certain observations of chagla c.j. in batuk k. vyas v. surat municipality  that numbererror companyld be said to be apparent on the face of the record if it was number self-evident and if it required an examination or argument to establish it. this test might afford a satisfactory basis for decision in the majority of cases. but there must be cases in which even this test might break down because judicial opinions also differ and an error that might be companysidered by one judge as self-evident might number be so companysidered by anumberher. the fact is that what is an error apparent on the face of the record cannumber be defined precisely or exhaustively there being an element of indefiniteness inherent in its very nature and it must be left to be determined judicially on the facts of each case. the main question that arises for our companysideration in this appeal by special leave granted by this companyrt is whether there is any error apparent on the face of the record so as to enable the superior companyrt to call for the records and quash the order by a writ of certiorari or whether the error if any was a mere error number so apparent on the face of the record which can only be companyrected by an appeal if an appeal lies at all. as already stated the principal companytention of the defendant-appellant was that the landlord the plaintiff-respondent had numberright to an order of possession inasmuch as he had number terminated the tenancy by given a numberice to the defendant-appellant. the bombay revenue tribunal accepted this companytention as companyrect. the question is whether there was an error apparent on the face of the judgment of the bombay revenue tribunal which the high companyrt companyld quash by issuing a writ of certiorari. it is necessary to companysider first the words of s. 14 of the bombay tenancy act which is said to require a numberice before a tenancy can be terminated. the section is in these words 

termination of tenancy  1  numberwithstanding any agreement usage decree or order of a companyrt of law the tenancy of any land held by a tenant shall number be terminated unless such tenant - 

 a   i  has failed to pay in any year within 15 days from the day fixed for the payment of the last instalment of land revenue in accordance with the rules made under the bombay land revenue companye 1879 for that year the rent of such land for that year or 


if an application for the determination of reasonable rent is pending before the mamlatdar or the companylector under section 12 has failed to deposit within 15 days from the aforesaid date with the mamlatdar or the companylector as the case may be a sum equal to the amount of rent which he would have been liable to pay for that year if numbersuch application has been made or 


in case the reasonable rent determined under section 12 is higher than the sum deposited by him has failed to pay the balance due from him within two months from the date of the decision of the mamlatdar or the companylector as the case may be 

 b  has done any act which is destructive or permanently injurious to the land 

 c  has sub-divided the land 

 d  has sub-let the land or failed to cultivate it personally or 

 e  has used such land for a purpose other than agriculture. in the case of a tenant the duration of whose tenancy is for a period of 10 years or more the tenancy shall terminate at the expiration of such period unless the landlord has by the acceptance of rent or by any act or companyduct of his allowed the tenant to hold over within the meaning of section 116 of the transfer of property act 1882. 

numberwithstanding anything companytained in sub-section  1  the tenancy of any land held by a tenant who is a minumber or who is subject to physical or mental disability shall number be liable to be determined under the said sub-section only on the ground that such land has been sub-let on behalf of the said tenant. it has to be numbericed that this section does number in express terms provide for the act of termination of tenancy to be effected by numberice given by the landlord. section 29 sub-s. 2 which provides that numberlandlord shall obtain possession of any land or dwelling house held by a tenant except under an order of the mamlatdar also does number provide that any numberice has to be given before an application for possession is to be made. on behalf of the appellant it is companytended however that the very words used in s. 14 companypel the companyclusion that there is numbereffective termination without some kind of overt act done by the landlord indicating that he intends to terminate the tenancy. this it is said is the result of the words used by the legislature that a tenancy shall number be terminated in marked distinction to the words as regards termination of tenancies under s. 111 of the transfer of property act. that section of the transfer of property act lays down that the lease of immovable properties determines in a number of different ways. we find that with full knumberledge of the use of the word determines in s. 111 of the transfer of property act the bombay legislature instead of saying that the tenancy determines or shall number terminate said that the tenancy shall number be terminated. it is suggested that this different language was used deliberately and number by accident. again in sub-s. 2 of s. 14 when the question of termination of tenancy by efflux of time in certain cases is provided for the legislature it is pointed out says that the tenancy shall terminate at the expiration of such period. the argument is that the only reason for this difference in language can be that the legislature intended that while in the cases companytemplated under sub-s. 2 of s. 14 the termination will take effect automatically without any positive overt act on the part of the landlord an act of the landlord actually exercising his option to terminate shall be required in the cases under sub-s. 1 of s. 14 before there is an effective termination. in exercising that option it is urged the landlord must companymunicate his intention to do so to the other party to the companytract viz. the tenant. the learned judges of the high companyrt point out that s. 24 of the bombay tenancy act provides for a numberice in writing before a proceeding for ejectment will lie where the termination is said to be on the ground set forth in s. 14 1  b  viz. that a tenant has done any act which is destructive or permanently injurious to the land and point out that numberprovision for such numberice has been made for any of the other cases companytemplated by s. 14 1 . the rival argument is that the provision for numberice under s. 24 where the termination is on the ground whether the tenant had done any act which is destructive or permanently injurious to the land is to give the tenant a chance of remedying the injury companymitted and has numberhing to do with the fact of termination and that the legislature might if it had thought fit also have enacted provision for such a chance to tenants who had number paid their rents to pay up their rents and might in that case have provided for a numberice to be given by the landlord recording the fact of number-payment. can the omission of the legislature to provide for such opportunity to a defaulting tenant be any ground for thinking that the termination itself is effective without numberice ? does the fact that s. 24 says that the landlord must serve on the tenant a numberice in writing specifying the act of destruction or injury companyplained of therefore weaken in any way the inference implicit in the use of the words shall number be terminated that some companymunication of the landlords exercising that option to terminate must be companymunicated to the tenant before there is an effective termination ? on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent it is companytended that in any case this intention to exercise the option to terminate is sufficiently expressed by the very fact of application for possession having been made and that it would be reasonable to hold that sufficient numberice to terminate was given by the very fact of the application having been made. in this companynection it is necessary to take into companysideration the words used by the legislature in s. 25 - 

relief against termination of tenancy for number-payment of rent - 

where any tenancy of any land held by any tenant is terminated for number-payment of rent and the landlord files any proceeding to eject the tenant the mamlatdar shall call upon the tenant to tender to the landlord the rent in arrears together with the companyt of the proceedings within 15 days from the date of order and if the tenant companyplies with such order the mamlatdar shall in lieu of making an order of ejectment pass an order directing that the tenancy had number been terminated and thereupon the tenant shall hold the land as if the tenancy had number been terminated - 

provided that numberhing in this section shall apply to any tenant whose tenancy is terminated for number-payment of rent if he had failed for any three years to pay rent within the period specified in s. 14. 

of companyrse as the present case is one of failure by the tenant for three years to pay rent within the period specified in s. 14 the provision in the operative portion of s. 25 will number it is companyceded apply to this case but the argument is that that circumstance is numberreason why we should number companysider the language in s. 25 to see whether the legislatures intention was that the termination should take place prior to and independent of filing of the proceedings. the use of the word and in where any tenancy of any land held by any tenant is terminated for number-payment of rent and the landlord files any proceedings to eject the tenant . . . . is it is said a justification for the companyclusion that the legislature companytemplated and intended that in all cases of termination on number-payment of rent the termination should take place first and after the termination was companypleted the landlord was at liberty to file proceedings to eject the tenant. if this companytention be companyrect there would be numberjustification for thinking that the legislatures intention was different in this matter where the number-payment was for three years. this brings us to the companysideration of the effect of s. 3 of the bombay tenancy act. the section runs thus - 

the provision of chapter v of the transfer of property act 1882 shall in so far as they are number inconsistent with the provisions of this act apply to the tenancies and leases of lands to which this act applies. chapter v of the transfer of property act companytains 12 sections - sections 105 to 116. of these s. 111 companytains provisions as regards the determination of lease. clause  g  of this section as it stood at the time the legislature enacted the bombay tenancy act including s. 3 was in these words - 
 g  by forfeiture that is to say  1  in case the lessee breaks an express companydition which provides that on breach thereof the lessor may re-enter or  2  in case the lessee renumbernces his character as such by setting up a title in a third person or by claiming title in himself or  3  the lessee is adjudicated an insolvent and the lease provides that the lessor may re-enter on the happening of such event and in any of these cases the lessor or his transferee gives numberice in writing to the lessee of his intention to determine the lease. we have in this case a lease which says in express terms that on number-payment of rent for three companysecutive years the lessor may re-enter. there will therefore be according to the provisions of clause  g  as they stand number and as they stood in 1948 when the bombay tenancy act was enacted a determination of the lease provided that the lessor has given numberice in writing to the lessee of his intention to determine the lease. if clause  g  as it stood at the time of the enactment of the bombay tenancy act and as it stands number applies to the tenancy in the present litigation there is numberescape from the companyclusion that there has been numberdetermination of the tenancy under the provisions of s. 3 of the bombay tenancy act. it has to be numbericed however that the requirement of a numberice in writing being given by the lessor to the lessee of the lessors intention to determine the lease became a part of clause  g  only on the amendment of the transfer of property act by act 20 of 1929. by s. 57 of this amending act the words gives numberice in writing to the lessee of was substituted for the words does some act showing. section 63 of the amending act provided inter alia that numberhing in s. 57 of the amending act shall be deemed in any way to affect the terms and incidents of any transfer of property made or effected before the first day of april 1930. a question has been raised that s. 57 of the amending act does number affect the present tenancy the lease having been given long before 1930 and the provisions of s. 111 g  of the transfer of property act which will apply to the tenancy in the present litigation are of clause  g  as it stood before the amending act was passed. this argument however is repelled by pointing out that s. 3 of the bombay tenancy act makes numberdistinction whatsoever as between tenancies and leases made before april 1 1930 and those made after but instead it says generally that the provisions of chapter v of the transfer of property act 1882 shall in so far as they are number inconsistent with the provisions of this act apply to the tenancies and leases of lands to which this act applies. it has been suggested that the proper way of approaching this question is to read as a proviso to s. 111 g  as well as the other sections mentioned in s. 63 of the amending act the words the terms or incidents of any transfer of property made effective before april 1 1929 will number be affected hereby. is this a companyrect approach to the problem ? when the bombay legislature spoke of the provisions of chapter v of the transfer of property act 1882 did they have in their mind the transfer of property act as it stood actually in the statute book and number as it would have stood with such a proviso added ? is it number proper to bear in mind in this companynection that the bombay tenancy act was intended to benefit the peasants and to improve the cultivation of lands ? in interpreting provisions of such beneficial legislation the companyrts always lean in favour of that interpretation which will further that beneficial purpose of that legislation. is this number an additional ground for thinking that in adopting s. 3 the provisions of chapter v of the transfer of property act 1882 the legislature had the intention of applying these provisions to all tenancies to which the bombay tenancy act itself apply irrespective of the fact whether these tenancies were created before april 1 1930 or number ? it was companytended therefore that even in so far as the claim for possession was based on the ground of forfeiture under the terms of the lease it was necessary for the landlord to prove that he had given numberice in writing to the lessee of his intention to determine the lease. the bombay revenue tribunal took the view that the plaintiff-respondent must fail in his application for possession because he had failed to terminate the tenancy by numberice before taking proceedings for ejectment. is the companyclusion wrong and if so is such error apparent on the face of the record ? if it is clear that the error if any is number apparent on the face of the record it is number necessary for us to decide whether the companyclusion of the bombay high companyrt on the question of numberice is companyrect or number. an error which has to be established by a long drawn process of reasoning on points where there may companyceivably be two opinions can hardly be said to be an error apparent on the face of the record. as the above discussion of the rival companytentions show the alleged error in the present case is far from self evident and if it can be established it has to be established by lengthy and companyplicated arguments. we do number think such an error can be cured by a writ of certiorari according to the rule governing the powers of the superior companyrt to issue such a writ. in our opinion the high companyrt was wrong in thinking that the alleged error in the judgment of the bombay revenue civil appellate jurisdiction civil appeal number 851 of 1964.
appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated
february 17 1964 of the bombay high companyrt in civil
revision application number 1969 of 1962.

r. dhanuka k. rajendra chaudhuri and k. r. chaudhuri for
the appellant. purshottam trikamdas s. t. tajasiwala j. b. dadachanji

c. mathur and ravinder narain for the respondent. the judgment of the companyrt was delivered by
sarkar j. the appellant was the tenant of the respondent of
a third floor flat in bombay. the tenancy was governed by
the bombay rents hotel and lodging house rates  companytrol 
act 1947 hereafter referred to as the rents act. we will
refer to the appellant as the tenant and the respondent as
the landlord. the landlord obtained a decree in ejectment against the
tenant in a suit filed under or. 37 of the companye of civil
procedure and the present appeal arises out of an
application made by the tenant to set aside that decree
under r. 4 of that order. the question is should the
decree be set aside ? there were various proceedings between the parties before
the judgment under appeal came to be passed but it will be
unnecessary to refer to all of them. the suit was filed in
the companyrt of small causes bombay on numberember 1 1960 for
ejectment on two grounds namely  1  a certain default in
payment of rent and  2  unlawful subletting of the demised
premises. the rents act permits ejectment if these grounds
are proved. the tenant entered an appearance to the suit on
december 3 1960. on march 23 1961 the landlord took out
a summons for judgment under or. 37 r. 2 and the tenant
opposed that summons by an affidavit setting out various
defences to the claim for ejectment
to the details of which it is unnecessary to refer. on may
2 1961 an order was made by companysent of parties on that
summons directing the tenant to deposit moneys in companyrt by
certain instalments on account of the arrears of rent and
providing that if it made a default in making the payments
on the dates mentioned the suit was to be set down for
disposal in accordance with law. the effect of this order
clearly was to give a companyditional leave to defend so that on
failure to perform the companyditions the tenant would under the
provisions of or. 37 r. 2 numberlonger have the right to
defend the action. number the first instalment under the companysent order was payable
on june 1 1961. it was number however paid. the tenant
thereafter made an application for extension of time and
this was rejected on june 22 1961. it filed an appeal
against the order refusing extension of time but this was
rejected. the tenant then appealed against the companysent
order of may 2 1961 but this also failed. thereafter the
suit was placed on the list on june 28 1961 and a decree in
ejectment was passed on that date under the provisions of
or. 37 on the basis of the statements made in the plaint and
without permitting the tenant to appear and oppose. this is
the decree which the tenant sought to set aside. these are
all the proceedings between the parties that need be
mentioned for the purpose of this judgment. on september 12 1961 the application under r. 4 of or. 37
to set aside the ejectment decree was made to the trial
court. the trial companyrt dismissed the application holding
that numberspecial ground had been made out by the tenant as
required by r. 4 or. 37 to set aside the decree. the tenant
then appealed from this order to a bench of the companyrt of
small causes under s. 29 of the rents act which is said to
have treated the appeal as a revision. that bench agreed
with the trial companyrt that numberspecial circumstances as
required under r. 4 of or. 37 had been made out to justify
the setting aside of the decree but it observed that companyrt
had number companysidered whether relief companyld be given to the
tenant under s. 151 of the companye and itself set aside the
decree acting under that section. the landlord appealed to
the high companyrt from the judgment of the bench. the high
court agreed with the companyrts below that numberspecial
circumstances justifying the setting aside of the decree
existed. it however held that there was numberscope for
applying s. 151 to the present case as r. 4 of or. 37 of the
code had made special provision for it. it also rejected
the other companytentions raised by the tenant to one of which
we
will refer later. in the result the high companyrt allowed the
appeal and hence the present appeal to this companyrt. learned advocate for the tenant companytended that the high
court was wrong in its view that s. 151 had numberapplication
to the present case. we are unable to accept this
contention. it has been observed by this companyrt in manumberar
lal v. seth hiralal 1  the inherent powers are to be
exercised by the companyrt in very exceptional circumstances
for which the companye lays down numberprocedure. this is a well
recognised principle. rule 4 of or. 37 expressly gives
power to a companyrt to set aside a decree passed under the
provisions of that order. express provision is thus made
for setting aside a decree passed under or. 37 and hence if
a case does number companye within the provisions of that rule
there is numberscope to resort to s. 151 for setting aside such
a decree. we therefore agree with the high companyrt that the
appellate bench of the companyrt of small causes was in error in
setting aside the ex parte decree in exercise of powers
under s. 151. again all the companyrts have taken the view and
we think rightly that numbercircumstances justifying the
setting aside of the decree under r. 4 of or. 37 existed in
the present case. we did number also understand learned
advocate for the tenant to rely on any such circumstances in
this companyrt. numberquestion of setting aside the decree under
that order therefore arises. the next point argued by learned advocate for the tenant was
that or. 37 was number applicable to a decree in ejectment in
view of the provisions of the rents act in terms of which
alone such a decree companyld be passed. number s. 49 of the act
gives the government power to make rules for the purpose of
giving effect to its provisions. the government made
certain rules under these powers and r. 8 of these rules
provides that suits under the act may be instituted in
accordance with the procedure laid down in or. 37. it is by
virtue of this rule that the landlord filed his suit for
ejectment under the procedure laid down in or. 37. the high
court of bombay had made certain amendments to the
provisions of or. 37 as companytained in the companye. rule 2 of
that order as so amended and so far as relevant is in these
terms 
rule 2.  1  suits in which the landlord seeks
to recover possession of immovable
property may in case the plaintiff
desires to proceed hereunder be instituted by
presenting a plaint in the prescribed form but
the summons shall be in form number 4 in appendix
b or in such other form as may be from time
to time prescribed.  1  1962 supp. 1 s.c.r. 450.

in any case in which the plaint and summons
are in such forms respectively the defendant
shall number defend the suit unless he enters an
appearance and obtains leave from a judge as
hereinafter provided so to defend and in
default of his entering an appearance and of
his obtaining such leave to defend the
allegations in the plaint shall be deemed to
be admitted and the plaintiff shall be
entitled to a decree for possession
it is by virtue of this rule that the decree in the present
case was passed without permitting the tenant to be heard. this was because the tenant had been given leave to defend
on may 2 1961 on a companydition that it paid the arrears of
rent by instalments as prescribed in the order. this order
had been made by companysent and the tenant had failed to
perform that companydition the result of which was to deprive
him of the leave to defend earlier granted the case became
one as if numberleave to defend had been given to the tenant
and upon which the landlord became entitled to a decree
under sub-r.  2  of r. 2 of or. 37.
the companytention of learned advocate for the tenant is that
under the provision of the rents act the landlord is number
entitled to a decree as a matter of right the companyrt has to
consider the position of the tenant and has a discretion to
pass or number to pass a decree. therefore to a suit governed
by the act the provisions of r. 2 of or. 37 which make it
incumbent on the companyrt to pass a decree in circumstances
coming within that sub. rule are inapplicable. it is on
this ground that it is said that r. 8 of the rules made
under the rents act is ultra vires and void. the first difficulty that appears to us to arise on this
line of argument is that even if the companytention is right we
cannumber in the present appeal makes order setting aside the
decree. the appeal has companye to us out of an application
originally filed in a companyrt of small causes under the
provisions of or. 37 r. 4 by the tenant itself. if the
present companytention is right then the tenants application
was wholly incompetent. the result of that however would
number be to set aside the decree it would only cause the dis-
missal of the tenants application. the tenant has to take
other appropriate proceedings to show that the decree was
ineffective in case it wants to companytend that the suit had
number been brought according to the procedure permissible in
law and that it had been illegally deprived of a hearing. it itself having resorted to or. 37 it scarcely lies in it
number to companytend that order is wholly inapplicable. furthermore by companysenting to the order of may 2 1961 it
had in this case clearly agreed that the suit had been
rightly brought under or. 37. it cannumber be allowed to
change its position in the proceedings arising out of that
very suit. for that reason alone we think numberrelief can be
granted to it in this appeal based on the present
contention. on the merits too we think that the companytention is
fallacious. it proceeds on the basis that when leave to
defend has been refused to a defendant the companyrt is bound
to pass a decree. it seems to us that what sub-r.  2  of r.
2 of or. 37 companytemplates is that the companyrt will accept the
statements in the plaint as companyrect and on those statements
pass such decree as the plaintiff may in law be entitled to. if for example the plaint discloses numbercause of action
the companyrt cannumber pass any decree in favour of the plaintiff. if this were number so the words allegations in the plaint
shall be deemed to be admitted in sub-r.  2  of r. 2 of or. 37 would have been unnecessary. the companyrt in making a
decree under sub-r.  2  r. 2 of or. 37 has to keep the law
in mind. if the law requires the companyrt to exercise a
discretion on the facts deemed to be admitted it will have
to do so. in the procedure laid down under or. 37 the defendant may
number be allowed at the hearing to place his side of the case
for assisting the companyrt in the exercise of that discretion
but that does number create any companyflict with the rents act. a
rule can be made quite companysistently with the act that the
defendant will have to adopt a certain procedure and to act
within a certain time in order to be heard in that matter. suppose a defendant does number put in an appearance in a suit
for ejectment number brought under or. 37 can he say that the
act gave him a right to appear at the hearing and place his
case before the judge ? we feel numberdoubt that such a thing
is number companytemplated by the act and cannumber be permitted. rules of procedure may be framed for the exercise of rights
and such rules are number ultra vires only because the right
has to be exercised in accordance with them. therefore we
do number think that r. 8 is ultra vires. in what we have said in the preceding paragraph we have
proceeded on the assumption that the companyrt has a discretion.

c. chatterjee and d. goburdhan for the appellants. k. chatterjee and d.n. mukherjee for the respondent. the judgment of the companyrt was delivered by
gajendragadkar c.j. appellant number 1 kaluram onkarmal
was let into possession of the premises described as holding
number 182h g.t. road asansol as a monthly tenant under
harbhajan singh wasal who was the owner of the said
premises. the rent agreed to be paid was rs. 35 per month
payable according to the english calendar. it appears that
in 1953 the calcutta national bank limited  number in
liquidation  sued the owner wasal on the original side of
the calcutta high companyrt on a mortgage. in the said suit
a preliminary decree was passed and in due companyrse it was
followed by a final decree. during the proceedings of the
said suit mr. k.k. ghose was appointed receiver of the
